title: Germany invades Poland
subtitle: The invasion and the battle for time
author: Ostfront Atlas
location: Poland and the Free City of Danzig
summary: Germany’s overwhelming advantages met effective resistance at bridges, fortified positions and village railway lines. The opening campaign turned on how quickly each army could move, recover and respond.
sourceMethod: The chapter compares German operational reporting with Polish military scholarship, museum accounts and contemporary diplomatic documents. Kennedy’s 1956 U.S. Army study is used for command assignments and identified operational reports, not its discredited cavalry-charge story or claims that Polish aviation was eliminated in the opening days. Reported advances describe leading units, not verified daily control boundaries. Disputed loss totals and Wieluń raid timings are qualified. Source notes identify the evidence and its limits.

sections.label: Mokra and the price of delay

body:
At Tczew, the German invasion began with an attempt to keep something standing. The bridges over the Vistula were worth more to an advancing army intact than as wreckage in the river, and the Polish defenders had prepared to destroy them. Before dawn on 1 September 1939, German aircraft attacked the installations that would make demolition possible while a railway operation attempted to deliver troops to the crossings. The plan joined air power, surprise and transport in a single effort to save time. It failed. Warned of the approaching danger, Polish personnel frustrated the seizure, and the bridges were blown during the morning. Germany had begun its war with overwhelming advantages, but one of the first important results was a Polish success.

The attack on Tczew, usually placed at approximately 4:34 a.m., preceded the familiar bombardment of Westerplatte. It also introduces the central problem of the campaign more clearly than a photograph of a battleship can. German forces needed crossings, usable roads and opportunities to get behind Polish formations before those formations could withdraw. Polish commanders needed time to complete concentration, bring reserves forward and establish a defence that could survive the opening blows. A demolished bridge could interrupt that process for the attacker; a breakthrough elsewhere could make the interruption insufficient for the defender. The first day was fought through this unequal contest over time. [1] [2] The agreement signed in Moscow on 23 August had made the strategic setting more dangerous for Poland. Germany could attack without expecting Soviet intervention to preserve Polish independence, while the secret protocol anticipated territorial rearrangements at Poland’s expense. Yet the bargain was neither a completed partition nor a joint timetable for the operations of 1 September. The Red Army had not invaded. Polish government, armies and population still occupied a country whose defeat remained a military objective, not an accomplished fact. This chapter follows the opening attack and the first days that revealed its momentum, stopping short of the separate Soviet invasion on 17 September. [3]

The order and the pretext

By the time German troops crossed the frontier, the machinery of aggression had been running for months. The army’s plan, Fall Weiss, aimed to destroy Poland’s armed forces before they could escape the converging German offensives. The disputes over Danzig and transit across the Polish Corridor provided the diplomatic setting, but the operational design reached far beyond a border adjustment. The destruction of Czechoslovakia earlier in the year had enlarged Germany’s southern approaches into Poland, giving military planners another direction from which to threaten the Polish rear. Their task was to exploit that geography quickly enough to prevent an effective defence from taking shape. [4] There had already been a false start. Hitler intended the offensive to begin on 26 August, then postponed it after developments including the formal Anglo-Polish alliance signed on the 25th. A German commando detachment failed to receive the cancellation in time and attacked the railway route near the Jabłonków Pass. Polish resistance defeated the attempt to secure the tunnel and station for the coming army. The episode belongs to the transition between diplomacy and war, and it exposes the practical character of the preparations: the seizure of infrastructure was important enough to put small advance parties across the frontier before the main formations arrived. [5] On 31 August, Hitler issued Directive No. 1 for the Conduct of the War. It specified the next day and 4:45 a.m. for the attack, including the operation against the Tczew bridges. Its opening language blamed an allegedly intolerable situation on Germany’s eastern frontier, but the document itself recorded a decision for force made in advance. The same directive restrained German action in the west, where Hitler wanted Britain and France to bear responsibility for widening the conflict. He was ordering a war against Poland while trying to control how other powers would enter it. [6] The public explanation depended on a manufactured reversal of responsibility. SS personnel staged an incident at the Gleiwitz radio station on 31 August to suggest a Polish attack on German territory. Nazi press instructions then required the invasion to be presented as a defensive response and discouraged calling it a war. Across the frontier, the realities were unambiguous: German formations had received offensive orders, assembled for offensive tasks and crossed into Poland. The false border incidents supplied an excuse for a decision already taken; they did not cause the movement of the armies. [7]

Inside the diplomatic record

Proposals the ambassador never received

On the afternoon of 1 September, Polish ambassador Józef Lipski told the American chargé in Berlin that he had not even been furnished with the German proposals supposedly offered as a basis for negotiation. This was Lipski’s account, recorded by the American diplomat, and it undercuts the image of a straightforward settlement rejected after normal discussions. The army was already advancing while diplomats were still documenting how the appearance of negotiation had been maintained.

[8]

Two armies, two different problems

Germany’s advantage was considerable, although campaign totals can conceal the conditions under which particular engagements were fought. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives approximately 1.5 million German troops, around sixty divisions and more than two thousand tanks for the invading force. A Polish museum estimate places the forces Poland fielded during September at about 900,000. These are broad campaign measures, not synchronized headcounts of men in their battle positions at dawn on the first day. Polish mobilization and concentration remained incomplete. Germany could choose the places where its strongest forces would strike; Poland was still assembling parts of the army with which it had to resist them. [9] [10] The difference in organization mattered as much as the total number of soldiers. German armoured and motorized formations were concentrated for operational tasks, supported by artillery, engineers, communications and the Luftwaffe. Much of the German army remained ordinary infantry, and the speed of its leading formations exceeded that of the forces following them. That division of labour was useful. Tanks could force a passage or move around resistance while following infantry engaged bypassed Polish troops and secured routes. A German spearhead did not have to conquer every place behind it before threatening the next important junction. The offensive acquired its momentum from the interaction of these forces, rather than from the performance of tanks in isolation. [4] [11] Poland possessed trained infantry, artillery and anti-tank weapons capable of defeating German attacks. Its cavalry formations were equipped to fight on foot, using horses for movement, and their weapons included machine guns, anti-tank rifles and 37 mm guns. The problem was getting sufficient force to the right place, keeping neighbouring formations in contact and preserving the ability to move when a position became untenable. A gun that could destroy a tank did not give its crew the operational mobility of an armoured division. A regiment holding its ground could still lose its supply route or find an enemy force approaching from the rear. Polish competence at the point of contact and German superiority across the theatre could therefore coexist. [12] The air comparison was harsher. The RAF Museum sets roughly three hundred mostly obsolete Polish aircraft against more than thirteen hundred German fighters and bombers. Polish squadrons had dispersed to field airfields before the attack, so the familiar story that the Luftwaffe destroyed them on the ground at the outset is false. Their survival allowed real resistance, but dispersal could not cancel the disparity in numbers, performance and capacity to sustain operations. Germany could commit aircraft against the fighting front, transport system and targets farther inside Poland while the smaller Polish force faced difficult choices about where to expend its strength. [13] Marshal Edward Rydz-Śmigły’s armies also faced a geographical problem for which there was no painless answer. A shorter position deeper in the country would have surrendered important industrial districts, population centres and access to the sea before a serious battle. A defence near the frontier committed troops to a broad arc threatened from the west, East Prussia and the south. The Polish plan tried to defend essential territory while preserving the possibility of withdrawal and continued resistance. Its success depended on time, communications and assistance from abroad—the very conditions the German offensive was intended to disrupt. [4]

Reading the offensive

Two German army groups directed the attack. **Army Group North**, under Fedor von Bock, brought together Third Army in East Prussia and Fourth Army in Pomerania. Georg von Küchler’s Third Army faced the Polish northern approaches, including the fortified position at Mława on the route towards Warsaw. Günther von Kluge’s Fourth Army attacked across the Corridor, seeking to cut off Polish formations and establish land communications with East Prussia. Within Fourth Army, Heinz Guderian’s XIX Corps supplied a powerful mobile striking force. The northern operation thus combined a drive into Poland with the practical need to connect two German concentration areas separated by Polish territory. [4] **Army Group South**, commanded by Gerd von Rundstedt, contained the heavier concentration and three armies. Johannes Blaskowitz’s Eighth Army advanced towards Łódź and protected the northern flank of the principal thrust. Walther von Reichenau’s Tenth Army, with the strongest concentration of armour in the offensive, drove from Silesia towards the interior and Warsaw. Wilhelm List’s Fourteenth Army attacked through the southern approaches towards Kraków and farther east. Their movements were related: the forces on either side helped protect Tenth Army’s advance while threatening Polish formations that might otherwise turn against it. A reader following only the arrow towards Warsaw would miss much of the work required to keep that arrow moving. [4] The Polish commands were arranged around the territory they had to defend. Army Pomorze under Władysław Bortnowski covered the Corridor; Army Modlin under Emil Krukowicz-Przedrzymirski faced the threat from East Prussia. Farther west and south stood Tadeusz Kutrzeba’s Army Poznań, Juliusz Rómmel’s Army Łódź and Antoni Szylling’s Army Kraków. Army Karpaty covered the southeastern approaches, the Narew Operational Group the northeast, and Army Prusy formed the principal strategic reserve. Their names are useful geographical guides, but the spaces between these forces were as consequential as their individual positions. Germany’s converging advances threatened to separate them, close their withdrawal routes and commit the reserves before those reserves were fully assembled. [4]

Slovakia made the southern threat more extensive. Its German-dependent government permitted the use of Slovak territory and committed forces of its own. Two Slovak divisions took part from 1 September, attacking towards places including Bukowina Tatrzańska, Krynica and Muszyna. Their contribution was much smaller than Germany’s, but it widened the area Polish commanders had to watch and defend. The political destruction of Czechoslovakia had become an immediate military disadvantage for Poland: the southern frontier now offered an attacker opportunities that had not existed in the same form a year earlier. [14]

Crossings and strongpoints

The operation at Tczew demonstrates why the rivers on an atlas need to be read as military obstacles. Aircraft could fly over the Vistula; the vehicles and supply columns required a crossing. German bombing sought to interfere with the demolition system, while the railway approach attempted to deliver a force before the defenders could destroy the bridges. Polish railway workers at Szymankowo helped raise the alarm and frustrate the surprise. Enough of the defensive arrangements survived for the bridges to be demolished. The German operation had failed in its immediate purpose even though aircraft and troops had reached their objectives. [1] [2] That distinction between reaching and possessing would recur throughout the campaign. A bridgehead needed to be held, a road kept usable and a crossing repaired or replaced before an army could exploit it reliably. German engineers could overcome obstacles, but doing so consumed equipment and hours. The Polish demolition at Tczew forced the invader to solve a problem its original plan had hoped to avoid. It did not halt Army Group North as a whole, whose other formations had different routes and tasks. The result was a significant local success within an offensive broad enough to absorb local failure. [11] Farther north, the battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on Westerplatte shortly before five in the morning. The Polish Military Transit Depot lay within the Free City of Danzig, and its defenders faced a concentration of firepower that appeared disproportionate to the small garrison. Major Henryk Sucharski commanded a force of a little over two hundred. The initial German assaults nevertheless failed, and the position remained in Polish hands at the end of the day. It would continue resisting until 7 September. Prepared defences and disciplined fire gave a small force an ability to survive that could not be inferred simply by counting men or comparing the size of their weapons. [15] [11] Mława presented a larger obstacle. Here the principal fortified position was defended by the Polish 20th Infantry Division within Army Modlin. Küchler’s Third Army encountered concrete defensive works, artillery and anti-tank fire after making progress earlier in the day. German infantry attacks met strong resistance; armour brought forward to break the position also failed to secure the expected result. The fighting continued on 2 September, while German forces sought opportunities to the east. The eventual threat to the defenders developed through outflanking and the deterioration of the wider position, rather than a simple repetition of the first frontal assault until Polish resistance disappeared. [16] For the Polish infantryman in a successful defensive position, this created a particularly bitter relationship between the visible and the unseen battle. Holding the ground immediately ahead could be entirely real. So could a threat developing beyond the unit’s field of view, where another formation had withdrawn or a gap had opened. An order to retreat could arrive after a day of effective resistance because the army’s position had changed elsewhere. German operational success repeatedly converted movement around a strongpoint into pressure upon its defenders. The advantage lay in being able to change the shape of the battle faster than the defender could restore a continuous position.

Mokra and the price of delay

At Mokra, northwest of Częstochowa, Colonel Julian Filipowicz’s Wołyńska Cavalry Brigade occupied ground between Army Łódź and Army Kraków. Its mission was to delay the enemy and maintain contact with neighbouring formations while the larger Polish deployment took shape. This was a professional assignment to a mobile covering force, and the terrain offered ways to carry it out. Woods restricted movement, the villages channelled approaches, and a railway embankment running along the eastern side of the position formed an obstacle to tanks. The brigade’s ability to use those features helped turn an apparent mismatch into a day of repeated German frustration. [17] The opposing 4th Panzer Division was a much stronger formation, with tanks, motorized infantry, artillery, engineers and supporting troops. Military historian Juliusz S. Tym gives its strength as 357 tanks; that is a divisional figure, not a claim that all those vehicles attacked the same Polish position simultaneously. The German advantage was therefore both substantial and more complicated than the image of a solid mass of tanks advancing against horsemen. Effective armour needed accompanying infantry and supporting fire. At several points the Polish defence exploited the vulnerability of tanks that had moved beyond adequate support, while German efforts became more coordinated as the day continued. [17] The Polish cavalry fought largely dismounted. Its anti-tank guns and artillery could engage the relatively lightly protected German vehicles, while the armoured train Śmiały added mobile firepower along the railway. Success required more than possessing the weapons: crews had to remain in action under bombardment, ammunition had to reach the guns, and threatened parts of the position needed support before they were overwhelmed. The terrain narrowed the choices available to attackers, allowing defenders to concentrate fire on approaches and openings. German assaults repeatedly entered dangerous ground without obtaining the decisive passage they needed. The brigade bought time through the use of weapons, terrain and local command. [12] It paid heavily for that time. Repeated attacks and bombardment wore down the defenders; positions had to be adjusted and units pulled back as pressure increased. The brigade’s subsequent withdrawal does not cancel what it accomplished on 1 September. Delaying forces are meant to interrupt an enemy’s timetable while retaining enough strength to continue fighting. Yet the reverse qualification is equally necessary: stopping a particular armoured division for a day did not restore the position of the whole Polish army. Other German formations could advance, and the defenders at Mokra still had to respond to developments outside the ground they had successfully contested. [17] [12]

Reading a battlefield total

A disabled tank is not always a destroyed tank

Published loss figures for Mokra vary, and a total of vehicles hit or temporarily disabled should not be presented as a count of permanent write-offs. Recovery and repair could return a tank to service. The securely established result is more useful here: the Polish brigade defeated repeated attempts at an immediate breakthrough. This account avoids turning disputed vehicle totals into an exact scoreboard.

[12] [17]
The related cavalry legend obscures a different engagement at Krojanty. There Polish cavalry charged German infantry, before coming under fire from armoured vehicles. The episode was transformed into the story of irrational horsemen attacking tanks with sabres, a convenient explanation that made Polish defeat appear to follow from national backwardness. The actual lessons of Mokra were harder for German propaganda to accommodate. Cavalrymen using modern anti-tank weapons could stop armour, and a supposedly irresistible formation could suffer a serious tactical check. Poland’s defeat requires an account of the larger military imbalance; a caricature of its soldiers explains very little. [10]

Measuring the advance

There is no honest single speed for the German advance on 1 September. Robert M. Kennedy’s U.S. Army reconstruction, drawing heavily on German operational records, reports that forward elements of Army Group South were three to four miles inside Poland by 6 a.m. and that some units had reached fifteen miles by late afternoon—roughly five to six kilometres and twenty-four kilometres respectively. These were advances by selected elements. They were not a uniform depth along the front, an army-wide daily average or proof that all the country behind the leading troops had been secured. The measurements describe how far particular parts of the offensive had progressed, alongside sectors where German attacks had been stopped. [11] The same account records destroyed bridges and damaged roads interrupting the southern advance during the afternoon. Those reports help explain the relationship between speed and preparation. A motorized column on a usable road could move rapidly; the same column halted at an obstacle became a problem for engineers and traffic control. Moving off the road might allow tanks to continue, but trucks, artillery and supply vehicles still needed a workable route. The appearance of movement at the front did not mean every part of the formation was keeping pace. Operational speed depended on closing those gaps often enough to maintain pressure. [11] A particularly instructive interruption came in the north on **2 September**. Kennedy records that armoured elements of XIX Corps temporarily outran their fuel and ammunition supply after the advance across the Brda. German supply columns had to fight through withdrawing Polish troops to reach the stalled tanks. This is a glimpse of vulnerability inside a successful offensive: the armoured point had moved faster than the system required to keep it fighting. Polish forces obtained only a temporary advantage, but the incident shows why a line drawn behind a spearhead cannot automatically be labelled secure territory. Enemy troops could remain between the tanks and their supplies. [11] By 3 September, the German Third and Fourth Armies had established contact across the Corridor, gravely worsening Army Pomorze’s position. In the south, the advance reached Kraków on 6 September, and the 4th Panzer Division reached Warsaw’s outskirts on the 8th. These milestones reveal a formidable capacity to exploit the opening battles, but arrival outside the capital did not mean possession of it. Warsaw continued to resist until 28 September. The contrast in dates measures the difference between a successful operational approach and the reduction of a defended city; it should not be collapsed into a claim that Poland had been defeated in a week. [11] [9]

An atlas distinction

What “24 kilometres” means

The reported fifteen-mile advance is an upper example for some Army Group South units by late afternoon on 1 September. It is not an end-of-day front line. The map therefore shows labelled command sectors and schematic directions, with separate markers for selected engagements. It does not fill in an invented band of conquered territory between the border and the arrowheads.

[11]
The uneven distribution of fighting also left Army Poznań comparatively little engaged at the outset. That did not make its soldiers irrelevant or its commander passive. German advances on either side increasingly threatened its position, forcing movement even where an immediate frontal attack had not broken its formations. Kutrzeba would later use the army’s remaining strength in the counteroffensive on the Bzura, beginning on 9 September. For the opening day, its situation illustrates a central feature of the invasion: an army could be compelled to leave ground by the danger of encirclement before the enemy defeated it on that ground. [11]

The war beyond the front

The destruction of transport and communications affected soldiers and civilians together. Air attack could delay reserves, interrupt a railway movement or make a road unsafe, while people fleeing the fighting entered the same transport network on which the army depended. To describe this only as interdiction would leave out the experience of those beneath the aircraft. At Wieluń, German bombing struck the town and its hospital on the first morning. An investigation by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance found that no Polish military units were present in the town on the eve of the invasion or on 1 September. The attack killed civilians, including hospital patients and personnel, far from any meaningful contest between equivalent military forces. [18] The exact timing of the first raid remains disputed, as does the complete number of victims. The investigation could document deaths but could not establish a final toll, and it challenged some higher figures repeated in commemorative accounts. The uncertainty over the clock and the count leaves the central findings intact: civilians were killed, patients and personnel died, and a hospital was struck in a town without the military units sometimes invoked to explain the raid. For the people beneath the bombs, the war arrived without the protection that even an inadequate defensive position might have offered. [18] [19] Violence also accompanied the ground forces. In the Parzymiechy area, close to the fighting south of Wieluń, Polish infantry resisted German troops through the first day before withdrawing towards Działoszyn. Paweł Żołądek’s research for the Institute of National Remembrance, based principally on witness testimony, describes German soldiers searching houses, seizing civilians and killing people during the occupation of the villages. Such actions belong inside the history of the advance. Treating the campaign only as a contest of arrows and formations can make civilians disappear at the very moment when the arrival of those formations transformed their lives. [20] Military advantage and civilian vulnerability intersected throughout the day, but they were not the same kind of inequality. A Polish gun crew might have a chance to defeat the tank approaching it. A hospital patient or a family seized from a cellar possessed no comparable means of resistance. The invasion must be understood at both scales: the army attempting to defend the country, and people exposed to bombing, flight and deliberate violence. The speed of conquest is one part of that history. What the conquerors did when they arrived is another, equally necessary part.

Nightfall and the widening war

Britain and France had not declared war when the first day ended. They demanded that Germany stop the attack and withdraw its forces, and the British parliamentary record of 1 September preserves the gap between that demand and the fighting already under way. Their entry into the war followed on 3 September. For Polish commanders, however, an allied declaration and effective military relief were different things. The Western powers did not mount a major offensive that could remove the immediate pressure on Poland; their longer strategy placed considerable weight on mobilization and economic blockade. Poland needed an intervention on the timescale of an army retreating under converging attacks. [21] [22] At nightfall on 1 September, the situation remained more complicated than the final outcome makes it appear. The bridges at Tczew had been destroyed, Westerplatte still resisted, Mława’s defences had checked German assaults and the Wołyńska Brigade had delayed a major armoured formation at Mokra. Other German units had made significant progress. Polish armies remained in the field, but the need to respond to simultaneous threats was already consuming their freedom of action. The first day had demonstrated both the capacity of Polish forces to fight effectively and the difficulty of translating separate tactical successes into a durable defence of the country. The German advantage lay in the number of problems it could force upon the defender at once. A halt in one sector could coexist with a dangerous penetration in another; formations that had held could be ordered back to avoid isolation; reserves could be drawn towards a crisis before they were ready. Every withdrawal then created further demands for transport, communication and coordination. Under those conditions, the initiative became cumulative. Germany’s offensive could survive failures that Poland, with fewer mobile resources and a threatened rear, had much less room to absorb. This is why 1 September deserves to be read as more than the ceremonial opening of a war whose outcome is already known. The day contained decisions, effective resistance, failed German plans and civilian disasters that the later sweep of the campaign can obscure. Poland had not surrendered or lost its sovereignty. Its armed forces were fighting to preserve the possibility of continuing the war, while Germany was trying to close that possibility faster than it could be rebuilt. Over the next fortnight the struggle would move deeper into the country. On 17 September, an invasion from the east would change its conditions again.
